title: The Mechanics of Teacher Burnout (AKA the Workload-Pressure Cycle)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In this article Stuart identifies the structural mechanics behind teacher burnout, which he calls the Workload-Pressure Cycle, arguing that naming and diagramming the cycle is the first step to escaping it. He draws on the World Health Organization's 2019 burnout classification, Emily and Amelia Nagoski's work on the stress cycle, and Chase Mielke's writing on the desire to quit teaching to provide a multi-faceted definition. Stuart's diagnosis is that burnout arises from two compounding forces: an unmanaged workload that accumulates pressure, and a failure to depressurize the self — body, mind, emotions, and relationships — before returning to that workload. The article argues that the correct first priority is depressurization of the self rather than workload reduction, because a calmer mind is better equipped to simplify and focus the workload. This piece introduces a multi-part series Stuart calls the 'depressurizing the teacher's soul' sequence, framing sustainability as a professional and personal imperative.
points: Burnout has a mechanical structure — the Workload-Pressure Cycle — that can be interrupted at two points: depressurize the self, and simplify the workload
The WHO defines burnout as energy depletion, increased cynicism about one's job, and reduced professional efficacy — all three are common in teaching
Stuart recommends starting with self-depressurization rather than workload reduction, because clarity comes first and enables better decisions about workload
Teaching from a burnt-out self produces a worse teacher and a worse life; Stuart's motivation for the series is explicitly relational — 'I like you'
The series promises to keep each post under 1,000 words so that the depressurization content does not itself become a source of pressure
